transcript.text: Hello, I am Commander Oscar Lazardi of the Santa Ana Police Department.
What you're about to view is a critical incident community briefing.
In the event of a critical incident, we strive to disseminate as much information as possible at the earliest opportunity,
contingent upon the progress of the investigation.
These briefings intend to provide the public with open and transparent communication
regarding officer-involved critical incidents.
These briefings are based on the facts we know at the time of the video briefing.
They contain information obtained from numerous sources, including but not limited to dispatch audio, video evidence, and witness or victim statements.

The Santa Ana Police Department takes the use of force by its officers very seriously and conducts thorough investigations into these incidents, often in conjunction with other investigative agencies.
These investigations typically require interviews with numerous witnesses, the review of video and audio evidence, and analyzing extensive amounts of forensic evidence.
As a result, these investigations can take up to a year to complete.
At this point in the investigation, no conclusions have been drawn concerning whether our officers acted consistently with our policies and the law.
Please be advised, critical incidents are often high stress and emotional for those involved.
As a result of this stress and emotion, audio and video recordings may contain strong language
and digital images may be graphic.
Warning, some viewers may find these videos disturbing and unsuitable for children.
Hello, I am Officer Natalie Garcia, the Public Information Officer for the San Ana Police
Department.
I will give you a brief overview of an incident that occurred on January 15, 2025.
At 1 p.m., Santa Ana police officers arrested an adult male at 1600 East 1st Street for trespassing,
felony defrauding an innkeeper, and resisting slash delaying a peace officer.
During the arrest, officers utilized a device referred to as the RAP, given the circumstances they faced.
The RAP is a temporary restraining device designed to increase officer safety.
reduce the risk of liability, and protect individuals during law enforcement interventions
when subjects are violent or potentially violent. The RAP may be utilized in situations when violent
or combative behavior is anticipated to immobilize the subject, prevent injuries,
or for transportation purposes. Following the application of the RAP, the suspect was transported
for medical evaluation and medically cleared to be booked at the Santa Ana Jail. At approximately
6 p.m., the suspect was placed in a restraint chair at the Santa Ana Jail and then placed inside a
cell. The next day, on January 16th, at approximately 1.28 p.m., while being escorted to the Orange
County Jail, the suspect appeared to faint and briefly lost consciousness. Correctional officers
immediately called for a nurse assigned to the jail and positioned him on his side to aid his
breathing. While receiving medical evaluation, the suspect regained consciousness but was

uncooperative and belligerent The suspect was placed in a restraint chair with a spit mask and moved to his cell for further medical evaluation At some point jail staff determined the suspect did not appear to be breathing so they immediately removed him from the restraint chair and initiated CPR
Orange County Fire Authority personnel responded and transported the suspect to the hospital where, despite medical life-saving efforts, he was pronounced deceased at 2.38 p.m.
Officers from the Santa Ana Police Department are issued body-worn cameras to be worn at chest level to provide a general perspective of the officer.
When the body-worn camera is activated, it goes back 30 seconds and starts recording.
During this pre-record buffer, audio is not captured.
This feature is designed to capture police activity that occurs suddenly.
It is important to understand that an officer's actions can sometimes obscure the body-worn camera.
On the day of the arrest, Santa Ana officers arrived at a hotel at the request of management,
who reported a guest had been occupying a hotel room for over 10 days without paying.
Management provided the subject's identifying information and, based on a desire to prosecute,
agreed to sign a private party arrest form.
At approximately 12.43 p.m., officers went to the identified hotel room,
where for approximately 15 minutes, they attempted to negotiate with the subject to leave the premises.
At 12.58 p.m., several officers entered the hotel room to arrest the subject and a use of force occurred.
After the subject was handcuffed, officers used the rat for safety reasons.
They then transported the subject to Orange County Global Medical Center for medical assessment and treatment.
Involved officers were wearing body-worn cameras that were actively recording their interactions with the suspect.
The body-worn camera footage depicts two officers who were involved in the use of force.

At the San Ana Jail, all activities are recorded on video by various cameras throughout the facility,
capturing both correctional staff and inmates.
There are 16 cameras positioned in key locations, including pre-booking, booking, detox cells, and short-term holding cells.
While most of these cameras only record video, some are equipped with audio recording capabilities as well.

Despite the extensive camera coverage, it is important to note that there may be instances where cameras can be obscured or have blind spots, making it challenging to achieve complete coverage in a large area.
Currently, correctional officers at the Santa Ana Jail do not wear body-worn cameras.
You will now see relevant camera footage of correctional officers escorting the subject for transport to the Orange County Jail.
Pursuant to standard protocol and procedure, this in-custody death prompted an investigation by homicide detectives, internal affairs, and the OCDA's office.
The arrestee was identified as 38-year-old Freddy D'Angelo Washington of Ventura County.
He had prior arrests for possession of drug paraphernalia, possession of narcotics, use and under the influence of narcotics, driving with a suspended license, and several failures to appear.
It is our desire to be transparent during these investigations by sharing information with the public about critical incidents.
For the next several months, three concurrent and independent investigations will be conducted.
The Orange County District Attorney's Office will continue to investigate any possible criminal conduct by the officers and civilians involved.
The Santa Ana Police Department Internal Affairs Division will conduct an administrative investigation into whether the officers followed departmental policies and procedures.
The Santa Ana Police Department Crimes Against Persons Division will investigate alleged criminal conduct by the suspect.
These investigative units will continue interviewing any new witnesses that may come forward and complete forensic tests and an autopsy.
Upon the conclusion of the investigations, the Orange County District Attorney's Office
will determine whether, if any, charges should be filed against anyone involved.
This is an ongoing investigation and the Santa Ana Police Department Crimes Against Persons
Division is asking anyone with information to contact directly at 714-245-8390 or through
Orange County Crime Stoppers at 1-855-TIP-OCCS.
Thank you for taking the time to view this Critical Incident Community Brief.
